title: Tick-Borne Rickettsial Diseases: Treat First, Titer Twice
summary: Know why rickettsial diseases are treated before the lab can confirm them, how serology, smears and PCR confirm them later, and how Q fever phase I and II antibodies separate acute from chronic infection.

reviewer.note: Teaches Ch. 63 Hit 1 (empiric doxycycline), Hit 2 (sulfonamides), Hit 4 (morulae), Hit 5 (Q fever phases), Hit 6 (serologic confirmation) and Traps 1, 3, 4, 5. Checked against Biggs 2016 (CDC MMWR RR-65(2)) and Anderson 2013 (CDC MMWR RR-62(3)). Adds E. ewingii as a granulocytic Ehrlichia (register flag rv-morulae-ewingii). Not taught: “< 20% seropositive at presentation”, Weil-Felix (no source read), and select-agent status.

objectives: Explain why treatment for suspected tick-borne rickettsial disease is never delayed for lab results.
Interpret paired IgG IFA serology for rickettsial disease.
Use blood smears and PCR appropriately for Ehrlichia, Anaplasma and RMSF.
Distinguish acute from chronic Q fever by phase I and II antibodies.

scenes.title: Fever after a camping trip — wait for the titer?
scenes.altText: A patient card: fever, headache, low platelets, a week after hiking; a tick bite is not recalled. A serology order sits in a tray with “results in 1–2 weeks.” Question token: “Treat now or wait?”

cues.text: A hiker returns with fever, headache and low platelets. She doesn’t remember a tick bite.
Rickettsial serology is sent. The result will take days — and the first sample may well be negative.
Do you wait for the lab, or treat now? And how will the lab eventually confirm it?

scenes.title: Normal: who the tick-borne bacteria are
scenes.altText: Three cards: Rickettsia rickettsii (Rocky Mountain spotted fever) — infects endothelial cells; Ehrlichia chaffeensis — multiplies in monocytes; Anaplasma phagocytophilum — multiplies in granulocytes. In white cells they grow as membrane-bound clusters called morulae (schematic mulberry token). A fourth card: Coxiella burnetii (Q fever).

cues.text: Tick-borne rickettsial diseases are caused by small, obligate intracellular bacteria. Rickettsia rickettsii causes Rocky Mountain spotted fever.
Ehrlichia chaffeensis lives mainly in monocytes. Anaplasma phagocytophilum lives mainly in granulocytes.
Inside white cells, ehrlichiae and anaplasmae grow as tight clusters in membrane-bound vacuoles — called morulae, from the Latin for mulberry.
A cousin often taught alongside them, Coxiella burnetii, causes Q fever — with its own serology rules.

scenes.title: What changes: why the lab is late
scenes.altText: A timeline: illness day 0 → treatment decision on day 1–3. IgG antibody bar rises mostly in the second week. A card: “Early tests are often negative — never delay doxycycline waiting for results.” Doxycycline token for all ages, including children under 8. A crossed-out sulfonamide token: “can worsen disease.” A note: beta-lactams, macrolides, aminoglycosides and sulfonamides don’t work.

cues.text: Antibodies take time. Most patients only have raised IgG titers by the second week of illness — long after treatment decisions must be made.
So treatment is never delayed for laboratory confirmation, and it isn’t stopped just because an early sample is negative.
Doxycycline is the drug of choice for all tick-borne rickettsial diseases, in patients of all ages — including children under eight.
Many common empirical antibiotics don’t work, and sulfonamides can make the illness worse.

props.title: Doxycycline
lines: Drug of choice for all TBRD

scenes.title: In the lab: confirming it later
scenes.altText: Card 1, serology: IgG IFA on paired sera 2–4 weeks apart; a fourfold or greater rise confirms; a single IgG titer ≥ 64 only supports; IgM is not reliable alone. Card 2, blood smear (Wright–Giemsa) in the first week: morulae in monocytes suggest E. chaffeensis, in granulocytes suggest A. phagocytophilum (or E. ewingii) — insensitive, needs confirmation. Card 3, PCR: good on whole blood for Ehrlichia/Anaplasma; for R. rickettsii, blood PCR is less sensitive — tissue (skin biopsy) is better; draw before doxycycline. Card 4, Q fever: acute = phase II IgG predominates (fourfold rise); chronic = high, rising phase I IgG (typically ≥ 1:1024; Duke criterion > 1:800).

cues.text: Serology confirms rickettsial disease in hindsight. Paired IgG samples two to four weeks apart: a fourfold or greater rise confirms it. One titer of sixty-four or more only supports it, and IgM shouldn’t be used alone.

In the first week, a Wright–Giemsa smear may show morulae — in monocytes for Ehrlichia chaffeensis, in granulocytes for Anaplasma, or for Ehrlichia ewingii. It’s insensitive, and a positive still needs confirmation.
PCR on whole blood works well for Ehrlichia and Anaplasma. For Rocky Mountain spotted fever, blood PCR is less sensitive — a skin biopsy is better. Draw samples before doxycycline when you can.
Q fever flips phases: acute infection shows mainly phase two IgG; chronic infection shows a high, rising phase one IgG — typically one in one thousand twenty-four or more.

scenes.title: Three classic traps
scenes.altText: Trap card: “Wait for serology before treating suspected RMSF” is crossed out → “Start doxycycline immediately.” Trap card: “Chronic Q fever = high phase II titer” is crossed out → “Chronic = high phase I IgG.” Trap card: “Granulocyte morulae always mean Anaplasma” is crossed out → “Usually Anaplasma, but E. ewingii also infects granulocytes — confirm by PCR/serology.”

cues.text: Trap one: never wait for serology to treat suspected Rocky Mountain spotted fever. Start doxycycline right away.
Trap two: chronic Q fever isn’t marked by phase two. A high, rising phase one IgG is the chronic signal.
Trap three: morulae in granulocytes usually mean Anaplasma — but Ehrlichia ewingii infects granulocytes too, so confirm with PCR or serology.

props.title: ✗ “Chronic Q fever = high phase II.”
lines: ✓ Chronic = high, rising phase I IgG

props.title: ✗ “Granulocyte morulae always = Anaplasma.”
lines: ✓ Usually — but E. ewingii too; confirm

scenes.title: Treat first, titer twice
scenes.altText: Memory aid: “Treat first, titer twice” — start doxycycline, then confirm with two IgG samples showing a fourfold rise. And “Q fever: II is new, I is old.” A card lists where the aid breaks.

cues.text: Memory aid: treat first, titer twice. Start doxycycline, then confirm with two IgG samples. And for Q fever: two is new, one is old.

Where it breaks: some species make antibodies late; cross-reactions mean serology may not name the exact species; some chronic Q fever patients keep very high phase two titers; and PCR or biopsy can confirm earlier than paired sera.

props.label: Q fever: II = new, I = old

scenes.title: Takeaway
scenes.altText: Two tokens: “Doxycycline immediately for suspected TBRD (all ages) · never wait for the lab”, “Confirm: paired IgG ≥ 4-fold rise · morulae suggest Ehrlichia/Anaplasma · Q fever chronic = phase I”.

cues.text: Start doxycycline as soon as a tick-borne rickettsial disease is suspected, then confirm later with a fourfold IgG rise, PCR or morulae — and remember chronic Q fever means high phase one IgG.

props.label: Doxycycline now for suspected TBRD (all ages) · never wait for the lab
Confirm: paired IgG ≥ 4-fold · PCR · morulae · chronic Q fever = phase I

explanation.what: Plain language: these infections are treated on suspicion because the lab can only confirm them later. Scientific terms: tick-borne rickettsial diseases (RMSF, ehrlichioses, anaplasmosis) are caused by obligate intracellular bacteria; doxycycline is the drug of choice for all ages. Confirmation: fourfold or greater rise in IgG IFA titer between paired sera; morulae (intracytoplasmic microcolonies) in leukocytes; PCR. Q fever (C. burnetii): phase II antibodies dominate in acute infection, phase I IgG rises in chronic infection.
explanation.why: Antibodies usually appear in the second week, after treatment decisions must be made; delays lead to severe disease and death. Sulfonamides can increase severity. R. rickettsii circulates in low numbers in blood, so blood PCR is less sensitive than tissue.
explanation.measure: Paired sera 2–4 weeks apart; fourfold rise confirms; single IgG ≥ 64 supports; IgM not used alone. Wright–Giemsa smear in week 1 (insensitive). PCR on whole blood (Ehrlichia/Anaplasma) or tissue (spotted fever), ideally before doxycycline. Chronic Q fever: phase I IgG typically ≥ 1:1024 (Duke major criterion > 1:800).
explanation.differs: E. chaffeensis (monocytes) vs A. phagocytophilum and E. ewingii (granulocytes). Acute Q fever (phase II) vs chronic (phase I).
explanation.examAngle: Expect: empiric doxycycline, sulfonamide trap, fourfold rise, morulae cell type, and Q fever phase reversal.

comparisons.title: Ehrlichia chaffeensis vs Anaplasma phagocytophilum
comparisons.distinguisher: Cell type — then confirm by PCR/serology.

mnemonic.text: Treat first, titer twice — and Q fever: II is new, I is old.
mnemonic.explanation: Start doxycycline on suspicion; confirm with paired IgG; phase II marks acute and phase I chronic Q fever.
mnemonic.limitation: Some species seroconvert late; cross-reactions blur species; some chronic Q fever keeps very high phase II; PCR/biopsy can confirm earlier.

analogyLimitations: Cells and morulae are schematic, not real morphology.
Scrub typhus, Bartonella and epidemic typhus are not covered here.
takeaway: Start doxycycline as soon as a tick-borne rickettsial disease is suspected, then confirm later with a fourfold IgG rise, PCR or morulae — and remember chronic Q fever means high phase one IgG.

questions.stem: A child aged 6 has fever, headache, thrombocytopenia and a petechial rash after a summer tick exposure. Initial rickettsial IgG is negative. What is the best action?

options.text: Start doxycycline now and send a convalescent sample in 2–4 weeks
options.rationale: Correct. Treatment is never delayed for lab results, and early serology is often negative.

options.text: Withhold treatment because the IgG is negative
options.rationale: Incorrect. A negative acute sample does not exclude infection.

options.text: Give trimethoprim–sulfamethoxazole because the child is under 8
options.rationale: Incorrect. Sulfonamides can worsen disease; doxycycline is recommended at all ages.

options.text: Repeat the IgG daily until positive
options.rationale: Incorrect. Paired sera 2–4 weeks apart are needed; treatment should not wait.

questions.stem: Paired IgG IFA titers against R. rickettsii are 1:32 (acute) and 1:256 (convalescent, 3 weeks later). How should this be interpreted?

options.text: Confirmed infection — fourfold or greater rise
options.rationale: Correct. 1:32 to 1:256 is an eightfold rise in a compatible illness.

options.text: Probable only, because the acute titer is below 1:64
options.rationale: Incorrect. Confirmation depends on the rise, not the first value.

options.text: Past infection, unrelated to the current illness
options.rationale: Incorrect. A rising titer indicates recent infection.
Incorrect. IgM should not be used alone; IgG paired sera are the standard.

questions.stem: A patient with a prosthetic valve and prior Q fever has phase I IgG 1:4096 and phase II IgG 1:1024. What does this suggest?

options.rationale: Correct. High, rising phase I IgG (≥ 1:1024) indicates chronic infection.
Incorrect. Acute infection is dominated by phase II antibodies.
Incorrect. These titers are high and suggest chronic disease.
Incorrect. Phase I/II antibodies refer to C. burnetii.

claims.text: Doxycycline for all TBRD at all ages; never delay for lab results; sulfonamides can worsen disease; common empirical antibiotics ineffective.
Paired IgG 2–4 weeks apart; ≥ 4-fold rise confirms; single IgG ≥ 64 supportive; IgM not alone; IgG mostly by week 2.
Morulae: monocytes (E. chaffeensis), granulocytes (A. phagocytophilum, E. ewingii); smear insensitive, needs confirmation.
PCR on blood good for Ehrlichia/Anaplasma; RMSF blood PCR less sensitive, tissue better; doxycycline lowers PCR yield.
Q fever: acute phase II predominates; chronic phase I IgG ≥ 1:1024 (Duke > 1:800).
Weil–Felix test is obsolete; < 20% seropositive at presentation; C. burnetii usually acquired by inhalation.
